issues.legal_issue: A court may convict fewer than five accused persons of an offence based on membership in an unlawful assembly only where the evidence establishes that at least five persons participated and the case has a proper evidentiary and charging basis for the additional members.
material_facts: The prosecution’s first information report named seven alleged participants and did not mention any others, although some witnesses gave vague evidence that 40 or 50 people took part.
Four of the seven accused were acquitted, leaving three appellants convicted with the aid of the common-object provision.
The High Court assumed that the assembly included persons who had not been tried but did not fully examine the evidence or determine whether an assembly of five or more persons existed.
issues.conclusion: Conviction of fewer than five persons is legally possible if the required basis for finding an assembly of five or more is established. The High Court had not made the necessary findings in this case, so the case had to be decided afresh.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, fewer than five accused may be convicted if the evidence establishes an unlawful assembly of five or more persons and the additional members are supported by an adequate charging and evidentiary basis. Where the charge does not identify additional members, the first information report and evidence, or other evidence, must establish their participation without prejudice to the accused. The Court relied on Topandas v. State of Bombay, R. v. Plummer, Bharwad Mepa Dana v. State of Bombay, Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, Sunder Singh v. State of Punjab, Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab, and Krishna Govind Patil v. State of Maharashtra; it approved Harchandra v. Rex.

predicates.collective_offense_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal involving a conviction based on alleged membership in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.charge_and_accepted_evidence_identify_ad: The charge identifies additional, potentially unidentified members of the assembly, and the court accepts evidence establishing their participation.
predicates.report_and_evidence_show_additional_memb: The report and evidence establish additional members despite their omission from the charge, and that omission has not prejudiced the accused.
predicates.other_evidence_shows_additional_members_: Evidence other than the report establishes additional members despite their omission from the charge, and that omission has not prejudiced the accused.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an unlawful-assembly conviction and one of the stated bases establishes additional members without prejudice, fewer than five accused may be convicted for offences committed by the assembly.

issues.legal_issue: A person cannot be held liable through common-object liability for an act attributed to a person whose acquittal has become final.
material_facts: The High Court considered the fatal shot to have been fired by a person acquitted at trial.
That acquittal was not challenged on appeal.
The High Court used the common-object provision to hold the appellants liable for the fatal act.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the fatal injuries were caused by the acquitted person, the High Court could not hold the appellants liable for that act by resorting to section 149 of the Indian Penal Code.
issues.legal_principle: An acquittal is effective for all purposes when the case involving that person is considered in an appeal by convicted co-accused; a convicted person cannot be held constructively liable under section 149 of the Indian Penal Code for an act attributed to the acquitted person. The Court relied on the principles in Topandas v. State of Bombay, R. v. Plummer, Bharwad Mepa Dana v. State of Bombay, Sunder Singh v. State of Punjab, Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab, and Harchandra v. Rex. The Court did not decide whether the exception discussed in Sunder Singh concerning incidental consideration of an acquitted person’s membership was consistent with Plummer.

predicates.collective_liability_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction based on alleged collective liability for an offence committed by an assembly.
predicates.acquitted_person_is_attributed_the_act: The act for which liability is asserted is attributed to a person who was tried and acquitted.
predicates.acquittal_is_final: The acquittal of the person attributed with the act has not been set aside on appeal.

issues.definition: In an appeal involving collective liability, if the act is attributed to a person whose acquittal is final, the convicted persons cannot be held liable for that act.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court considering collective-liability convictions must determine whether an unlawful assembly existed, what acts its members committed in furtherance of its common object, and whether the appellants participated before deciding their liability.
material_facts: The High Court was not satisfied with the trial court’s treatment of the case but assumed that an unlawful assembly existed.
It did not fully examine the evidence to decide whether at least five persons other than the acquitted persons formed an unlawful assembly.
It did not determine the particular acts committed in furtherance of the common object or whether any appellant participated in the incident.
issues.conclusion: The High Court failed to determine essential questions. The Supreme Court set aside its judgment and remanded the case for a fresh decision.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court must examine the evidence and make definite findings on whether an unlawful assembly existed, the acts committed by its members in furtherance of the common object, and the participation of the appellants before deciding whether collective liability applies. Section 423(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was discussed in connection with appellate powers, but the Court expressed no opinion on whether the interpretation in Sunder Singh was consistent with R. v. Plummer. The Court also relied on the principles stated in Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab and the other authorities concerning unlawful assembly and collective liability.

predicates.collective_liability_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal involving convictions based on alleged membership in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.appellate_court_has_not_determined_assem: The appellate court has not examined the evidence and reached a definite conclusion about whether an unlawful assembly existed.
predicates.appellate_court_has_not_determined_membe: The appellate court has not determined what acts members committed in furtherance of the common object and whether the appellants participated.

issues.definition: When an appellate court in a collective-liability appeal has left assembly membership, member acts, and appellant participation unresolved, its judgment must be set aside and the case remanded.
